title: Dow Gains 300 Points as S&P 500, Nasdaq Rebound from Lows Amid Easing Tech Selloff
body:
U.S. equity markets nudged higher on Wednesday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average climbing roughly 300 points, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite each rebounded from recent lows. The modest rally came amid a backdrop of mixed signals: technology stocks continued to feel pressure, yet the broader market found some breathing room after the latest personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index confirmed that inflation remains above the Federal Reserve’s 2 percent target, reinforcing expectations for further rate hikes.

The Dow’s ascent was led by a handful of heavyweight industrials that posted solid earnings, including a rise in defense contractor orders and a modest uptick in consumer‑discretionary sales. The index closed at 35,842, up 300.6 points, or 0.84 percent, marking its best daily gain in three weeks. The broader S&P 500 followed suit, finishing 0.6 percent higher at 4,527, while the tech‑laden Nasdaq added 0.5 percent to settle at 14,102. Despite the gains, the Nasdaq’s recovery was modest, as semiconductor makers and cloud‑service providers continued to shed value after a string of disappointing quarterly results.

Technology shares, which have been the primary drag on market sentiment this month, posted a net decline of 0.8 percent. Chipmaker Intel fell 2.4 percent after analysts highlighted weaker-than-expected demand for its data‑center products, while software giant Microsoft slipped 1.6 percent following a cautious outlook on its Azure growth. Even so, the sector’s sell‑off showed signs of easing; trading volume in the tech index was down 15 percent from its peak earlier in the week, suggesting that investors may be pausing to reassess the depth of the downturn rather than fleeing the space entirely.

The PCE data released earlier in the day showed a year‑over‑year increase of 4.7 percent, marginally above the 4.6 percent forecast and well above the Fed’s comfort zone. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy, rose 5.3 percent, reinforcing the central bank’s view that inflationary pressures remain entrenched. In response, Treasury yields edged higher, with the 10‑year note climbing to 4.31 percent, its highest level since early 2023. Higher yields have traditionally weighed on growth‑oriented stocks, particularly in the tech sector, by inflating discount rates used in valuation models.

Analysts note that the market’s resilience, despite the inflation data, reflects a growing belief that the Federal Reserve may adopt a more measured approach to tightening. “Investors are balancing the reality of stubborn inflation with the understanding that the Fed cannot keep raising rates indefinitely without risking a recession,” said Laura Chen, senior economist at Capital Insights. “The modest bounce in the Dow and S&P suggests that the equity market is pricing in a possible pause or a slower pace of hikes after this quarter’s data.”

Looking ahead, market participants will keep a close eye on the upcoming earnings season, especially the results from the remaining big‑tech names slated to report later this week. In addition, the Federal Reserve’s policy meeting scheduled for next month will be a focal point, as policymakers are expected to signal whether the current trajectory of rate hikes will continue or give way to a more dovish stance. For now, the modest gains across the major indices indicate that while inflation concerns remain, the market is finding room to breathe, setting the stage for a potentially volatile but opportunistic trading environment in the days to come.
